title: Astrophotography Anomaly Detector
blurb: Median-stacks a night-sky session to reject transients, then differences the frames to flag streaks — a meteor or satellite caught crossing the field.

steps.say: Point a camera at the night sky for a while and most of what you capture is the same stars, frame after frame. The interesting thing is what appears in only one frame — a meteor, a satellite. This tool finds those with classical computer vision: no neural network, just frame differencing and a Hough transform.
Three frames from a single fixed-tripod session, loaded in order. Here is the first.
Detect anomalies. It compares consecutive frames and runs a Hough transform over the differences to pull out straight streaks that a stack of stars alone would never produce.

One streak flagged, with a cropped preview and its measured length and angle. Notice the label: possible meteor or satellite trail — never a confident verdict, because telling those two apart from position drift alone is genuinely unreliable, and the tool refuses to pretend otherwise.

And here is why the detection is trustworthy: the median stack. Take the pixel-wise median across every frame and the transient simply vanishes — it was an outlier at its pixels — while the stars, present in every frame, survive untouched. The streak the tool flagged is exactly what the median threw away.

The honest limits: this assumes a static tripod and compares frames exactly as uploaded — no star-based alignment or plate-solving — and it deliberately won't call a streak a meteor versus a satellite. Always eyeball the cropped preview; it points you at candidates, it doesn't certify them.
